beats.caption: Every flash cell has a glass film a few nm thick
beats.text: Inside each NAND or NOR cell, a sheet of silicon dioxide separates the channel from the charge store. It is about 7 to 10 nm thick, a few dozen atoms. All data in flash depends on this layer.

beats.caption: It sits between the channel and the floating gate
beats.text: Below it is the silicon channel between source and drain; above it is the floating gate that holds the bit. At normal voltages it is a near-perfect insulator, so stored electrons stay for ten years or more.

beats.caption: High voltage: electrons tunnel straight through
beats.text: Put about 20 V across the film and the barrier bends thin enough for electrons to tunnel through quantum mechanically (Fowler-Nordheim tunnelling). Program sends them up; erase reverses the field to pull them back.

beats.caption: Each cycle leaves damage: traps build up
beats.text: Electrons forced through the oxide break bonds and leave charge traps behind. Traps shift thresholds and open leak paths, so retention drops. This is the main reason a cell survives only thousands of cycles.

beats.caption: Thinner is faster but leakier
beats.text: Thinning the oxide lowers write voltage but lets charge leak; that limit helped push NAND from shrinking cells to stacking them in 3D. Oxide deposition and etch: Applied Materials (AMAT), Lam Research (LRCX); users: Micron (MU), Samsung (005930.KS).
